parts.title: PreFold-dG: estimating how strongly two proteins stick together, using the in-between information a protein-folding model produces
parts.abstract:
Abstract

Motivation

How strongly two proteins stick together, which scientists call binding affinity, controls how proteins interact, and it lies behind many essential processes in living things. Researchers have built computer methods to simulate and predict how proteins bind. However, there is very little high-quality data, and this has held these methods back a great deal. As a result, most methods try to predict how binding affinity changes when one protein is changed by a mutation (a single-letter change in its building-block sequence). This change is written ΔΔG. Few methods try to predict the binding affinity itself, written ΔG. Working this way risks overfitting, which means a model learns the quirks of a lopsided set of data too closely and then does worse on new cases.

In recent years, computer programs have become much better at predicting the 3D shape of proteins. These programs can now model the shapes of proteins on a large scale, and they give us rich information about structure, which can largely explain how proteins bind. Even so, using these advances to predict binding affinity has not yet led to reliable predictions.

Results

We present PreFold-dG, a model that estimates the binding affinity of protein pairs. It uses in-between information, called intermediate embeddings, from Boltz-2, a free, open-source program that predicts protein shapes. Our approach gathers information about each amino acid (each building block of a protein) and gives more weight to amino acids that are closer together in space. It predicts ΔG directly, rather than predicting the change in binding affinity, ΔΔG.

PreFold-dG reached the best performance so far on well-established tests of binding affinity prediction, and it held up well on separate test sets. We also ran ablation studies, in which we removed one piece of information at a time to see how much each piece mattered. These suggest that the model uses all of the intermediate embeddings to make its predictions, although how much each one contributes differs between predicting ΔΔG and predicting ΔG. Finally, we checked our model on real-world data from CR6261, a broadly neutralizing antibody (an antibody that can block many different strains of a virus), whose mutations matter for how the virus has evolved.

Availability

https://github.com/LGAI-Research/PreFold-dG.
parts.introduction_first:
Proteins are the basic working units of life, and the ways they interact with one another, called protein–protein interactions, play a central role in what cells do. Measuring how strongly two proteins bind, their binding affinity, therefore matters both for understanding the basic science of molecules and for practical work such as finding new drugs and redesigning proteins.

The classic way to estimate binding affinity is to start from a crystal structure, a detailed 3D picture of the proteins taken from a crystal grown in the lab. From that picture, physics-based scoring tools such as FoldX (Delgado et al. 2019) or Rosetta Flex-ddG (Barlow et al. 2018) calculate how well the proteins fit together. These methods are grounded in physics, but they often need a lot of computing power and are not very accurate at predicting.

Recent progress in predicting protein shapes, most notably AlphaFold3 (Abramson et al. 2024), has made it possible to model protein structures accurately on a large scale. Since then, a growing number of models have used these predicted structures, together with protein sequences or protein language models (computer programs that learn patterns in protein sequences), to estimate binding affinity. Despite this progress, current methods still face several basic limitations.
parts.conclusion:
4 Conclusion

Proteins are the basic units of what living things do, and the way proteins bind to one another supports a huge range of processes inside cells. Predicting binding affinity accurately therefore matters both for understanding how molecules interact and for practical uses such as designing antibodies as medicines (Bang et al. 2025).

In this study, we present PreFold-dG, a model that estimates binding affinity using the in-between information that Boltz-2 produces. We gather this information into compact summaries, giving more weight to amino acids that are closer together in space. We also split the task of predicting the change in binding affinity (ΔΔG) into two separate predictions of binding affinity itself (ΔG). With these steps, PreFold-dG reaches the best performance so far on the major tests.

We also showed that the model captures real biological patterns. In CR6261, whose mutations matter more for how the virus has evolved, we reproduced two patterns. The first is epistasis, where the effect of one mutation depends on other mutations. The second is pleiotropy, where a single mutation affects several things at once. We hope this work can be extended to other properties, such as predicting how stable a protein is, and we encourage further research where protein shape prediction meets the modeling of physical and chemical properties.
parts.introduction_rest:
Most existing models predict the change in binding affinity (ΔΔG) when a protein is mutated, rather than binding affinity itself (ΔG). This habit comes from the fact that measurements of binding affinity itself vary a great deal. Different laboratories use different lab tests and procedures, and these give different numbers (Sanavia et al. 2020).

ΔΔG is, by definition, a difference between two ΔG values: one for the mutant pair and one for the wild-type pair. The wild type is the original, unchanged version of a protein. If a model takes these two pairs and squeezes them straight into a single number using a hidden, unexplained calculation, it loses two things. First, the arithmetic no longer holds up. Second, the result is hard to explain.

There is a second problem. Because these models need both the wild-type and the mutant pair as input, they can only learn from cases where both have been measured together. That leaves out the large number of measurements in which only one pair was measured. On top of this, the ΔΔG values in the test collections are lopsided: most are small, and a few are very large. With so few examples to learn from, the model may struggle to understand the full range of binding affinities. More broadly, because these models always need a wild-type pair as a reference, they cannot be used at all when designing proteins from scratch, where no such starting point exists.

In this work, we propose two key ideas to tackle these problems.

First, we rewrite the task of predicting ΔΔG in its natural form. We predict the ΔG of the mutant pair and the ΔG of the wild-type pair, each by the same part of the model, and then take the difference. Because the two predictions come from the same model, the rules of arithmetic are built in. If the mutant binds more strongly, the mutant's ΔG is lower, and the difference is negative. If the wild type binds more strongly, the difference is positive. The model also obeys transitivity: if the mutant beats the wild type, and the wild type beats a third pair, then the mutant beats that third pair. Each ΔG prediction can also be checked on its own (Montanucci et al. 2022). To deal with the differences between lab measurements, we also rescaled the target values using a normalization step, which puts them on a common scale. This reduces the mismatches between results from different studies.

Second, we do not rely on the final 3D shapes that protein shape prediction programs produce. Instead, we use the in-between information (intermediate embeddings) from Boltz-2 (Passaro et al. 2025), one of the first free, open-source programs that runs AlphaFold3, as the ingredients for estimating ΔG.

Proteins that bind to each other are always moving. A single predicted shape is only one snapshot of the many slightly different ways the proteins can sit together while bound. The in-between information, by contrast, has not yet been boiled down into one final shape. It may therefore keep richer information about how the amino acids interact than the final shape alone. Other recent work agrees with this view. Some researchers have tried to predict binding affinity from how confident a protein shape prediction is (Nori et al. 2025). Others have tried to work out a combined shape that represents all the possible bound states, so that the model can predict information about several states at once (Kalakoti and Wallner 2025).

Our approach reaches the best performance so far on the test collections and on separate test sets, and it holds up well on new cases. Because it predicts ΔG directly, it also lets us predict each ΔG on its own. This may make it easier to use more data in the future and to apply the method to designing proteins from scratch. We also analyze how the model works and present case studies that show how useful it is in practice.
parts.methods:
2 Methods

2.1 How we set up the problem

We measure the binding affinity of a protein pair by comparing its Gibbs free energy (ΔG) when the two proteins are bound together with its Gibbs free energy when they are apart. Gibbs free energy is a measure of how much energy a system has available to do work. The change in binding affinity is written ΔG = G_bound − G_unbound. A negative value means the proteins bind on their own, without any outside push.

We compare a mutant pair, where one protein has been changed by a mutation, with the wild-type pair, which is the original, unchanged pair. The change in binding affinity caused by the mutation is then:

ΔG_mut = G_mut,bound − G_mut,unbound
ΔG_wt = G_wt,bound − G_wt,unbound
ΔΔG = ΔG_mut − ΔG_wt

Because the same method is used for both pairs, any bias that comes from the method itself cancels out. What is left shows directly whether the mutation helps the proteins bind or makes binding harder. For this reason, most existing computer methods treat the task as a paired-input problem: they take the mutant and the wild-type together and predict the change in binding affinity:

f: (mutant, wild-type) → ΔΔG

However, this approach mixes the information about the mutant and the wild-type inside a "black box" model, one whose inner workings are hard to inspect. In this work, we instead split the task into two separate predictions of binding affinity itself, one for each pair:

h: (protein complex) → ΔG

ΔΔG = h(mutant) − h(wild-type)

Splitting the task like this gives two useful mathematical properties. The first is anti-symmetry: ΔΔG_wt→mut = −ΔΔG_mut→wt. In words, if we swap the direction of the mutation, the predicted value simply flips its sign. The second is transitivity: ΔΔG_A→C = ΔΔG_A→B + ΔΔG_B→C. In words, the prediction does not depend on which route we take through the space of possible sequences. Both properties follow automatically from computing ΔΔG as the difference between two ΔG values. Ordinary model designs do not guarantee either property unless extra design rules are added (Deng et al. 2025). Splitting the task also lets us look at each ΔG prediction, and the in-between information behind it, on its own. This makes the model's behavior more transparent and easier to understand.

2.2 Where our data came from

SKEMPI 2.0 (Jankauskaitė et al. 2019) is the most widely used test set for predicting how binding affinity changes when a protein is mutated. It contains 7085 ΔΔG measurements that were checked by hand. They come from 345 PDBs, which are entries in the Protein Data Bank, a public collection of protein structures. The measurements cover single mutations and mutations at several places, in many different protein pairs. The binding affinities were measured with various lab tests, such as SPR (surface plasmon resonance), ITC (isothermal titration calorimetry) and ELISA. SKEMPI contains duplicate entries, and measurements from different studies can disagree. We deal with both of these in the preparation steps described in Section 2.3.

To test our model fairly, we also used a separate test set: the HER2 binder dataset, which GearBind (Cai et al. 2024) took from experimental measurements (Shanehsazzadeh et al. 2023). It contains 417 mutations on different versions of an antibody that targets HER2, a protein on the surface of some cancer cells. All of these mutations come from a single structure, entry 1N8Z. This entry also appears in SKEMPI, but the two datasets are quite different. SKEMPI mostly contains single mutations that replace one amino acid with alanine, a small amino acid. The HER2 dataset, by contrast, includes many mutations at several places, and its ΔΔG values are spread out in a different way. This makes it a test set of new cases, outside the range of what a model trained on SKEMPI has seen, so we can check how well such a model generalizes.

2.3 Preparing the data

SKEMPI contains duplicate entries, because the same measurement was repeated under different experimental conditions. We merged these using a filter applied one step at a time to each unique identifier, which is the combination of the PDB entry, the protein chains and the mutations. First, we kept only entries from the latest version of the dataset, preferring SKEMPI v2.0 over v1.0. Next, we sorted the experimental methods into three levels of reliability (Table S1) and threw out lower-level entries whenever higher-level data were available. When several measurements were still left, we took their median, the middle value, so that unusual results would have less effect.

Some entries share the same protein pair but have different mutations. Because measurements from different studies can disagree, the wild-type ΔG values for these entries may not agree with each other. To fix this, we worked out one agreed wild-type ΔG for each protein pair, using the same filtering and median steps. We then recalculated each mutant's ΔG by adding the reported ΔΔG to this agreed wild-type value:

ΔG_mut = ΔG_wt, consensus + ΔΔG reported

This step takes advantage of the fact that ΔΔG values are more reliable than ΔG values. It also makes the ΔG values consistent with one another across all entries in a PDB. After filtering and recalculating, our final dataset contains 5817 entries covering 334 different protein pairs.

2.4 Our model

As described in Section 2.1, our approach splits the prediction of ΔΔG into two separate predictions of ΔG, one for the mutant pair and one for the wild-type pair, using the same model for both. For each input, we use the in-between information from Boltz-2 (Passaro et al. 2025). This information comes as four tensors, which are simply arrays of numbers. They are s_inputs, s, z and distogram, and they are produced when Boltz-2 processes a protein pair. Table 1 describes what each one holds and how big it is. Here L stands for the total number of amino acids in all the chains (A and B) of the protein pair.

Table 1

The in-between information taken from the Boltz-2 protein shape model.

| Data | Shape | Description

| s_inputs | [L , 384] | First summary of each amino acid

| s | [L , 384] | Refined summary of each amino acid

| z | [L, L,128] | Summary of each pair of amino acids, based on their positions

| distogram | [L, L,64] | Summary of the distances between each pair of amino acids

L is the total number of amino acids in the proteins.

Figure 1 shows how our model, PreFold-dG, is built. We expect that how strongly two proteins bind depends mainly on pairs of amino acids, one from each protein, and that how much each pair contributes depends on how close the two amino acids are in space. For a protein pair (A + B), we first take the four in-between summaries from Boltz-2. Two of them, s_inputs and s, describe single amino acids. The other two, z and distogram, describe pairs of amino acids. To look at binding from the point of view of these pairs, we follow AlphaFold2 (Jumper et al. 2021) and multiply each amino acid's summary by every other amino acid's summary. In mathematical terms, this is called a self outer product along the amino acid axis. It produces arrays of shape [L,L,384×384].

Figure 1

An overview of PreFold-dG. Boltz-2 turns the proteins into in-between information, which is then passed to the part of the model that predicts binding affinity. One shared part predicts ΔG_mut from the mutant input and ΔG_wt from the wild-type input, and ΔΔG is the difference between the two.

Different proteins have different numbers of amino acids, so the size of these arrays changes from one example to another. To give every example the same size, we used the distogram to gather the information from s_inputs, s and z into a single summary, giving more weight to amino acids that are closer together. In practice, we work out the expected distance from the distogram. We then combine the three summaries with weights that are inversely proportional to the square of the distance (1/D² pooling). This is similar to how gravity works: the closer two things are, the stronger their pull. Pairs of amino acids on the same chain are left out and given a weight of zero. After this step, s_inputs and s are each reduced to shape [384×384], and z to shape [128], no matter how long the original protein sequences were.

Next, we pass the combined s_inputs and s through a linear layer, a simple set of weighted sums that shrinks them to a smaller space of numbers. This is followed by batch normalization, which keeps the numbers in a steady range, then a nonlinear activation, a step that lets the model learn curved relationships, and dropout, which randomly switches off some connections during training so the model does not lean too heavily on any one of them. For z, we use only dropout. All three summaries are then turned into a shared space of the same size. We combine the three by averaging them into one summary, which then passes through a two-layer MLP (a small stack of layers that learns to make a prediction) to estimate ΔG. The change in binding affinity caused by the mutation, ΔΔG, is found by subtracting the predicted ΔG of the wild-type pair from that of the mutant pair, both predicted by the same model.

Finally, we train the model by looking at all three predictions together: ΔG_mut, ΔG_wt and ΔΔG. For each one, we use the mean squared error, which is the average of the squared differences between the predicted and measured values. We add these three together as a single training score, called a loss, and adjust the model to make it as small as possible. Boltz-2 stays frozen during training, meaning its weights are not changed. This keeps its in-between information intact, separate from the part of the model that predicts binding affinity. Table S2 gives the full training settings and the choices we made for the model.
parts.results:
3 Results

3.1 Predicting the change in binding affinity (ΔΔG)

We tested PreFold-dG on the SKEMPI dataset, a large collection of protein pairs with measured changes in binding affinity, in two different ways of splitting the data. We also tested it on a separate dataset of binders to a protein called HER2. We report five scores.

Two of them measure how well the model's predictions line up with the measured values. The Pearson correlation coefficient (PCC) checks whether the predictions rise and fall together with the measurements. The Spearman rank correlation coefficient (SRCC) checks whether the model puts the mutations in the right order, from strongest to weakest binding. For both, 1 is a perfect match.

The other two measure the size of the errors. The root mean square error (RMSE) and the mean absolute error (MAE) both give the typical size of a prediction's error, so smaller is better.

The fifth score, the area under the ROC curve (AUROC), tells us whether the model gets the direction right. We sorted each ΔΔG into a simple yes-or-no answer, such as "binding gets stronger" or "binding gets weaker", and checked how often the model's answer matched the measurement.

These overall scores can be pushed up by a model that is good at telling apart protein pairs from different PDB entries, but poor at ranking mutations within the same protein pair. The PDB (Protein Data Bank) is the public database of protein structures, and each structure has its own ID number. To avoid this, we also report a per-structure PCC and SRCC. We calculated these within each PDB group that had at least 10 data points, and then took the average across groups, giving every group equal weight (a "macro-average"). This matches earlier studies. It gives a fairer picture of how well a model ranks mutations within the same protein pair (Wu and Li 2025). That skill matters directly for practical uses such as affinity maturation, where scientists make many small changes to a protein to make it bind more strongly.

3.1.1 Splitting by PDB entry

A simple random split can put mutations from the same PDB entry into both the training set and the test set. The model can then use the fact that the two look alike, and this makes it look better than it really is (Yu et al. 2025). To keep the two sets truly separate, Luo et al. (2023) proposed a 3-fold cross-validation scheme. In this scheme, the data are divided into three parts, and each part is held back in turn for testing. All mutations from the same PDB entry go into the same part. This split has been widely adopted and is now the standard benchmark.

We compared PreFold-dG with existing methods using this split (Table 2 and Table S3). PreFold-dG did better than the other methods on the per-structure scores and held up well on the overall scores. Most notably, its per-structure scores improved a great deal, and these scores are more reliable for practical use (Luo et al. 2023).

Our decomposition (Section 2.1) separates two things: the baseline energy of each protein pair, and the extra energy added or removed by each mutation. SKEMPI covers only a limited range of mutations, and its PDB entries are unevenly spread. Because of this, models that cannot capture the per-structure ΔΔG values tend to do poorly on protein pairs they have never seen (Wu et al. 2025).

3.1.2 Splitting by structural similarity

Splitting by PDB entry misses one case. Sometimes two protein pairs with identical or very similar structures are stored under different PDB IDs. Bushuiev et al. (2024) introduced a similarity-aware split to handle this. It groups protein pairs by how similar their contact surfaces are, and it holds back five proteins for testing. This reduces the chance that information leaks from the training set into the test set.

PreFold-dG did better than earlier methods on most scores. Compared with PPIformer, the best method in that study, its SRCC was 38% higher and its PCC was 46% higher (Table 3). Bushuiev et al. (2024) also noted that deep learning methods, and physics-based methods such as Flex-ddG, perform very differently from one protein target to another. PreFold-dG gave the most balanced predictions across these very different targets.

3.1.3 A separate test on HER2

To check further how well PreFold-dG works on new data, we tested it on the dataset of binders to HER2, following the method of GearBind (Cai et al. 2024). SKEMPI already contains several protein pairs related to HER2, so information could leak between the two datasets. To reduce this risk, we used the Smith–Waterman algorithm, a standard tool for measuring how similar two protein sequences are, to check how closely the two datasets were related (Fig. S1). We found nine PDB entries containing HER2 (Table S4) and left them out of training.

We split the remaining protein pairs into five parts, as GearBind does, and averaged the predictions across the parts. Table S5 and S6 show that PreFold-dG not only reached the best performance so far, but also had the most stable scores across the parts.

3.2 Predicting binding affinity itself (ΔG)

Our decomposition naturally gives an estimate of the binding affinity of each protein pair. Most ΔΔG models cannot do this without major changes to how they are built. To show this, we chose BA-DDG (Jiao et al. 2025) as a point of comparison. BA-DDG is built from separate parts, and it estimates the binding affinity of the wild-type pair (the original, unmutated proteins) and of the mutant pair separately. This makes it one of the few ΔΔG models that can be tested on binding affinity itself. We retrained BA-DDG to predict both ΔΔG and ΔG at the same time, using the same training method as ours (Section 2.4).

Table 4 shows that PreFold-dG predicts binding affinity well, both overall and per structure. BA-DDG also competes well overall, but its per-structure scores are weaker. Its ΔΔG scores also fell below those of the original model, which was trained only on ΔΔG labels (Table 2). This shows that predicting ΔG is a different challenge from predicting ΔΔG. It is not simply a side task that models built for ΔΔG can pick up along the way.

Table 4

ΔG scores on SKEMPI, using 3-fold cross-validation.

| Task | Method | Per-structure PCC ↑ | Per-structure SRCC ↑ | Overall PCC ↑ | Overall SRCC ↑ | Overall RMSE ↓ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| ΔG | BA-DDG | 0.361 | 0.350 | 0.634 | 0.612 | 1.916 |
| | PreFold-dG | 0.611 | 0.573 | 0.711 | 0.712 | 1.719 |
| ΔΔG | BA-DDG | 0.408 | 0.393 | 0.682 | 0.553 | 1.697 |
| | PreFold-dG | 0.611 | 0.573 | 0.750 | 0.660 | 1.602 |

Comparing the per-structure ΔG and ΔΔG scores gives a likely explanation. In principle, the two should give the same ranking, because the wild-type binding energy (ΔGwt) is just a fixed starting value that is added to or subtracted from. BA-DDG, however, is built on ProteinMPNN, a model that predicts protein sequences. The order in which ProteinMPNN writes out the wild-type amino acids depends on which mutant pair is given. As a result, BA-DDG quietly builds in the positions of the mutations, and it gives a different ΔGwt estimate every time. This creates the gap. The weaker per-structure scores also suggest a possible risk: the model may mix up the mutant and wild-type information.

Table 2 shows that physics-based methods such as FoldX and Rosetta Flex-ddG have very little gap between their overall and per-structure scores. This is natural, because they score each PDB entry on its own. Deep learning models show larger gaps. This suggests that part of their overall success comes from telling apart PDB entries, rather than from ranking mutations within a structure. PreFold-dG's gap falls in between. It keeps the ability of a learned model to capture detail, while relying less on shortcuts between PDB entries. We put this down to our explicit ΔG decomposition, which ties the predictions to individual protein pairs.

We also tested PreFold-dG on the Adaptyv competition data (Cotet et al. 2025). These data cover 24 targets, with measured KD values for binders that were designed from scratch. KD (the dissociation constant) measures how tightly a binder sticks: a lower KD means stronger binding. We tested two settings: (i) sorting binders from non-binders, and (ii) predicting KD values for the binders that worked.

Table S7 shows that PreFold-dG sorted binders from non-binders in a meaningful way on the largest targets. For EGFR (n = 768, AUROC = 0.69), NiV-G (n = 884, AUROC = 0.59) and PD-L1 (n = 75, AUROC = 0.72), the AUROC scores were 0.69, 0.59 and 0.72. This means that PreFold-dG carries over the rough binding signals it learned from SKEMPI to binders designed from scratch. However, it did poorly at the finer task of ranking binders, which matches how hard this task has been reported to be (Cotet et al. 2025). PreFold-dG's ΔG predictions on their own carry over to binders designed from scratch at a rough level, but more detailed predictions need further improvement.

3.3 Ablation studies

BA-DDG did worse when it was trained to predict both ΔG and ΔΔG. This suggests that our relabeling (Section 2.3) and the joint loss (the combined training goal) do not improve predictions on their own. Instead, they work together with particular design choices and in-between information. To separate out what each part contributes, we ran ablation studies on the input features and on the loss terms (Table S8).

Removing each of the three input features, s_inputs, s and z, made the model worse. This shows that each one captures a different side of binding affinity, even though they are linked in a chain. Removing z caused the smallest drop. This fits with z being a 128-number summary that is mainly used to store the distances between amino acids, which the model uses to build the structure. Removing s caused the largest drop in ΔΔG prediction, while removing s_inputs caused only a moderate drop.

This pattern does not hold for ΔG prediction, where removing s_inputs had the biggest effect. This fits our intuition that ΔG and ΔΔG depend on different sides of the input information. Modeling ΔΔG as a "delta" of ΔG can work well, but only when the model captures the features that matter for both tasks. We discuss what each input feature carries in Section 3.4.

Removing loss terms also made the model worse on most scores. The biggest drop came on the task linked to the training term we removed. In other words, each training term most strongly affected the task it was directly tied to. However, training only on ΔG hurt ΔΔG prediction less than training only on ΔΔG did, because ΔΔG naturally depends on ΔG. This supports our idea that a model properly trained on ΔG labels can, in principle, predict ΔΔG labels, but not the other way round.

Each wild-type structure is seen many times, once for each of its mutant versions, so the model may overfit to how they are represented. We checked how sensitive PreFold-dG is to the size of the wild-type binding energy (ΔGwt) in the joint loss. Table S9 shows that giving the wild-type term less weight brought no gain, and it made both ΔG and per-structure ΔΔG prediction worse.

3.4 What the in-between information carries

To see what information each feature carries, we looked at the in-between information from Boltz-2. For the features that describe single amino acids, we also used self outer products, which turn each summary into a table of how strongly each pair of amino acids is linked. We then used PCA (principal component analysis), a method that boils many numbers down to a few main directions of variation, to show the results as a picture (Fig. 2). To save computing time and to make sure we covered many different PDB groups, we used only wild-type protein pairs.

Figure 2

PCA of the in-between information from Boltz-2. The self outer products of s_inputs and s are labeled s_inputs2 and s2. s_inputs is clearly linked to amino acid type, and z is clearly linked to the distance between amino acids.

For single amino acids, s_inputs groups the amino acids by type, while s does not, even though s is much larger and varies much more. This suggests that the main directions of variation in s describe where amino acids are in space, rather than what they are. In a similar way to how language models work, s_inputs is like a fixed word description that does not change with context, while s is like a description shaped by the words around it.

For pairs of amino acids, z is directly linked to the distance between them, unlike s_inputs2 and s2. These observations reflect the order in which information flows through Boltz-2. From s_inputs, through s and z, to the distogram (a table of predicted distances between amino acids), the information is squeezed step by step, from 384 numbers to 128 to 64, toward the final goal of producing the 3D coordinates. As this squeezing happens, the information comes to describe distances more and more, and other factors drop away.

However, binding affinity depends not only on how the amino acids are arranged in space. It also depends on the information about each amino acid, shaped by its surroundings, that the in-between information carries. Existing models usually rely on the type of amino acid together with the predicted structure or the distances between pairs (like s_inputs plus the distogram). The summary s sits between these two. Models that use only the final structure cannot reach it.

Notably, Boltz-2 built its own binding affinity module from the second-to-last summary, rather than from the final distogram. Liu et al. (2025) showed that coordinates alone give only limited accuracy for the energy interactions between parts of a protein. AlphaFold3 also openly states a key limitation of protein shape prediction models: they predict fixed structures, not how proteins move and change (Abramson et al. 2024). We do not claim that the later summaries carry no useful information. But the shrinking number of numbers, together with the PCA results, suggests that relying only on the final, squeezed summaries risks throwing away rich information that matters for binding affinity.

3.5 A closer look at the CR6261 antibody

To test PreFold-dG on mutations that arose naturally and that act in groups, we chose the CR6261–H1 antibody–antigen dataset from Phillips et al. (2021). The researchers measured KD values for many combinations of mutations in a broadly neutralizing antibody against influenza. The mutations were of two kinds: somatic mutations, which arise during the antibody's development, and changes in the framework regions, the parts of the antibody that hold it together. This dataset covers 11 mutation sites, which give 2048 possible combinations, and 1844 of these have measured KD values.

We trained PreFold-dG on SKEMPI, leaving out hemagglutinins (Table S10), which we found by measuring how similar the sequences were (Fig. S1). PreFold-dG then predicted ΔG values on this held-out data, with an SRCC of 0.725, a PCC of 0.682 and an MAE of 2.190.

ESM-IF1 is a model that predicts protein sequences from protein shapes. Its log-likelihood, a score of how well a sequence fits the shape, has been used as a stand-in for ranking binding affinity without any labels. Its SRCC of 0.58 on CR6261-H1 (Shanker et al. 2024) shows what protein structure alone can recover. PreFold-dG reached an SRCC of 0.725 on the same dataset after we left out all SKEMPI protein pairs whose sequences were similar to H1/H9. That is 25% higher than the ESM-IF1 baseline. The gain reflects the extra information that comes from training on ΔG labels, compared with methods that rely only on structure.

We also checked whether the predictions reproduce the key biological findings of the original study (Fig. 3). The left panel shows the predicted ΔG values grouped by how many mutations each version has compared with the germline, the antibody's original starting sequence. The average predicted ΔG does not simply rise or fall. It first increases, meaning binding gets weaker, when there are few mutations, and then slowly recovers as more mutations are added. This fits the epistasis reported in the study, where only one of the eleven mutations helped H1 binding on its own.

Figure 3

A closer look at the CR6261 antibody. (Left) Predicted ΔG grouped by the number of mutations compared with the germline. The overall rise, with an early drop in binding affinity, captures the epistasis reported. (Center) Predicted versus measured ΔG, grouped by the mutation states of three amino acids that work together (T29P, S35R, S83F). (Right) Predicted ΔG of the same CR6261 versions binding to influenza H1 and H9, reproducing the pleiotropy observed.

Three of the mutations we chose, T29P, S35R and S83F, were reported to work together in binding. The center panel shows that pairs of these mutations (11,01,01,011) mostly bind more strongly than single mutations (10,00,10,001). The extra gain from all three together (111) is small, which reflects the "diminishing returns" reported by Phillips et al. (2021). We see this pattern in both the measured and the predicted values. It shows that the in-between information may quietly carry the spatial relationships that matter for such teamwork between mutations. Still, separating the information about structure from patterns that appear by chance in the data needs further study.

Finally, PreFold-dG's predictions for the same CR6261 versions binding to influenza H1 and H9 are strongly correlated (SRCC: 0.786; PCC: 0.796). This partly reflects the clear structural similarity between the H1 and H9 stem regions, the parts of the virus that the antibody grabs. Even so, it is encouraging that the model captures the pleiotropy in the combined data without any fine-tuning. Altogether, these results point to the potential of computer methods for exploring how binding affinity changes across many different evolutionary and functional settings. They also encourage further testing on a wider range of antibody–antigen systems.
